newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks close out the year on glum note.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks close out the year on glum note.

text.p: Tokyo stocks went out with a whimper on the last trading day of 1996, fluctuating nervously as players wondered what the New Year would bring for the Japanese economy and currencies.

The key Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed out the year with a marginal loss after clawing back from an early slide, but it still finished Monday's half-day session well below the level it settled exactly a year ago.

It was a subdued ending to a year which has seen the benchmark veering from a peak of 22,666.80 in the summer to a trough of 19,161.71 on Christmas Eve, reflecting the shifting state of the Japanese economy and the fortunes of the yen.
The Nikkei ended at 19,361.35, down 7.69 points or 0.04 percent from the previous session, and around 500 below its 1995 close.

The holiday-depleted market failed to shake off worries about whether the Japanese economy can sustain its already anaemic recovery into 1997, when tax rises will start to bite and supportive public spending will subside.

Renewed strength in the dollar on Monday provided an added incentive for foreign investors to sell stocks, by sapping their value in dollar terms. The greenback bobbed above 116 yen in Tokyo trade, coming close to a 44-month high of 116.20 yen set in New York on Friday.
"Sentiment was glum to begin with and it was aggravated further by the yen's tumble to 116 yen to the dollar," said Masaaki Higashida, a strategist at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

The uncertain outlook for the Japanese economy and sinking stocks have strengthened the view that Tokyo will have to keep its interest rates low to bolster the economy, sending investors flocking to the higher yielding dollar.

The Nikkei sank as much as 1.5 percent during Monday's session but pared losses to close almost flat as some players tried to push prices into positive territory to achieve a more auspicious finish for 1996. The stock market reopens after the New Year holidays on January 6.
Brokers said the gloom was likely to persist into 1997.
"The despondent atmosphere which has hammered stocks lower recently has not changed and probably won't change during the holidays," said Seiki Orimi, a Dai-ichi Securities analyst.
"The outlook on the economy is bleak, holding back investors lacking in confidence."

The Nikkei's feeble finale was in contrast to its highstepping entry into 1996. On the first day of trade on January 4 it leapt nearly 750 points to finish at 20,618.00, then the highest close since September 2, 1994.

A fall in the yen and signs that the sluggish economy was shifting into higher gear helped push the market up to a peak in the summer. But after hitting a 4-1/2 year closing high of 22,666.80 on June 26, the mood shifted.

Downward momentum escalated in December after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned of "irrational exuberance" on financial markets and investors began to brood over the impact of planned fiscal tightening on the Japanese economy in 1997.
On December 6, the Nikkei posted its steepest single-day plunge of the year falling 667.20 points, spooked by the idea of a U.S. interest hike and the fallout on Japan.
Despite repeated assurances from Japanese policy-makers that the recovery will be sustained, the Nikkei slumped to a 12-month closing low of 19,161.71 on Christmas Eve.
Investors fear that the government's tight budget for next year, incorporating nearly seven trillion yen ($61.4 billion) worth of tax rises, could tip the economy back towards slump. ($1=114)
